nameStory: Greater stitchwort gets its name from an old folk belief that it could heal wounds and 'stitch' them back together. The 'wort' part is an Old English word meaning 'plant' or 'herb,' found in many traditional plant names. It's also called 'starwort' because its white flowers look like tiny stars scattered through the woods.
description: Greater stitchwort is a delicate perennial wildflower that brightens woodland edges and fields with clusters of small white flowers. This sprawling plant grows 1-2 feet tall with weak, square stems that often lean on nearby plants for support. Its bright white, star-shaped flowers have five deeply notched petals that make them look almost like they have ten petals at first glance. Originally from Europe, it occasionally pops up in New England gardens and naturalized areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white flowers about half an inch across with five deeply split petals that create a distinctive star shape. Each petal is so deeply notched it almost looks like two separate petals, giving the flower a delicate, lacy appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. The leaves feel smooth and have a fresh, slightly bitter smell when crushed, with pointed tips and no teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Weak, sprawling stems that are distinctly four-angled or square when you roll them between your fingers. The plant often leans on or climbs through other vegetation for support.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, oval seed capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. The capsules make a subtle rattling sound when mature and dry if you shake the stem gently.

habitat: Look for greater stitchwort along woodland edges, in partially shaded gardens, and occasionally in open fields with rich, moist soil. It prefers areas with some protection from full sun and tends to grow among other low woodland plants and grasses. In New England, it's most likely to appear in cultivated or semi-naturalized areas rather than deep wild forests.

seasonality.spring: Bright white star-shaped flowers bloom from late spring into early summer, creating the most visible and identifiable stage of the plant.
seasonality.summer: Flowers continue blooming into summer, followed by the development of small seed capsules. The narrow leaves remain green and visible.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open. The above-ground parts begin to die back as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: The plant dies back to its roots, leaving little trace above ground except for dried stems in protected areas.

funFact: Despite being in the pink family, greater stitchwort produces purely white flowers - the family name comes from other members like carnations and pinks that do have colorful blooms, showing how plant families can surprise you with their diversity!
confusionNotes: Greater stitchwort is most easily confused with chickweed, which also has small white flowers and grows in similar areas. The key difference is that stitchwort's petals are much more deeply notched (almost split in half) and its stems are distinctly square, while chickweed has rounder stems and less deeply divided petals.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was recently moved from the genus Stellaria to its own genus Rabelera in 2019 based on genetic studies, so you might still find it listed as Stellaria holostea in older field guides. It's the only species in its new genus, making it quite unique from a botanical classification standpoint.
compareHints: Since greater stitchwort is the only species in its genus Rabelera, compare it to its pink family relatives like chickweed and mouse-ear chickweed. Greater stitchwort stands out with its much more deeply split petals (nearly divided in half), distinctly square stems, and larger flower size. While chickweeds have small, less showy flowers, stitchwort's blooms are more star-like and eye-catching.
